nodes.label: Elo Rating System
nodes.description:
Overview:
A method to assign each player a number (rating) that represents their skill level.

Expected Score:
E = 1 / (1 + 10^(–Δ/400)), where Δ = (your rating – opponent rating). This gives the probability you will win based on you and your opponents ratings.

Rating Update:
After a match, your rating changes by ΔR = K × (S – E), where:
• S = actual score (1 = win, 0.5 = draw, 0 = loss)
• K = sensitivity constant (larger K → bigger rating gains)

Why “Probabilistic”?
Instead of treating wins and losses as absolute, it uses probabilities—surprise (S–E) drives the update.

Key Innovations:
• First rating system grounded in probability theory
• Scales to thousands of players with simple arithmetic
• Incremental updates without re‐rating the entire pool

Source:
Arpad Elo, The Rating of Chessplayers, Past and Present (1978).

nodes.label: Paired Comparison Model
nodes.description: A method that estimates each competitor’s skill by analyzing outcomes of one-on-one contests. When two players face off, the model uses their win-loss record to adjust skill estimates. Example: if Alice wins 7 of 10 chess games against Bob, Alice’s skill rating increases above Bob’s.

nodes.label: Standard Deviation
nodes.description:
Measures how spread out values are around the mean. Calculated as:

σ = √( (1/N) Σᵢ (xᵢ – μ)² )

In a Gaussian (normal) distribution, σ sets the scale: about 68% of values lie within ±1σ, 95% within ±2σ, and 99.7% within ±3σ. Saying “1 standard deviation away” means one σ unit from the mean, not a fixed number—it scales with the dataset. In rating systems, this concept becomes “ratings deviation” (RD): both are σ measures, but standard deviation describes data spread in general, while RD specifically quantifies uncertainty in an individual player’s rating. RD decreases as more game results accumulate (greater certainty) and increases over time when inactive (more uncertainty). Example: if ratings follow a normal curve centered at 1500 with σ=100, ~68% of players score between 1400 and 1600.

nodes.label: Logistic Function
nodes.description:
A curve that turns any real number into a value between 0 and 1, making an ‘S’ shape. The basic formula is:

L(x) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ˣ)

• As x → +∞, L(x) → 1; as x → –∞, L(x) → 0; at x = 0, L(x) = 0.5.

In rating systems, we use a base-10 version:

E = 1 / (1 + 10^(–Δ/400))

where Δ is the rating difference. This converts Δ into a win probability. Example: if Δ = 100, then E ≈ 1 / (1 + 10^(–0.25)) ≈ 0.64, so the stronger player wins about 64% of the time.

nodes.label: Glicko Rating System
nodes.description: Extends <node id="0">Elo</node> by tracking both a player’s rating (r) and a <node id="29">ratings deviation (RD)</node> to quantify uncertainty. Each rating period updates in two steps: first, RD grows with inactivity via variance addition (RD_new = √(RD_old² + c²)), then both r and RD shrink with game results by combining prior and data variances (RD_new = √(1/(1/RD² + 1/d²))). Expected score E is computed using the <node id="3">logistic function</node> (E = 1/(1+10^(–Δ/400))) adjusted for both players’ RD, improving prediction accuracy. Finally, you express a player’s skill as a <node id="8">confidence interval</node> (r ± 1.96·RD for 95%), making uncertainty explicit. Example: a player with r=1500, RD=200 beats a 1400±30 opponent—r jumps and RD shrinks, reflecting gained information. Originally published by Mark E. Glickman in 1995.

nodes.label: Arithmetic Mean
nodes.description: The arithmetic mean (average) is the sum of all values divided by the number of values. It provides the central value around which deviations are measured. In standard deviation, each value’s distance from the mean (xᵢ – μ) is squared, summed, and averaged to quantify spread. Example: for scores {2, 4, 6}, the mean is 4, so deviations are {–2, 0, +2}, which feed directly into σ’s calculation.

nodes.label: Exponential Function
nodes.description: A mathematical function where a constant base is raised to a variable exponent. Commonly, f(x)=eˣ, which grows rapidly as x increases and decays when x is negative. In the logistic formula, e⁻ˣ creates the S-shaped curve by converting any real number x into a value between 0 and 1. Example: e⁻¹≈0.37, so L(1)=1/(1+e⁻¹)≈0.73.

nodes.label: Statistical Model
nodes.description: A mathematical framework that describes how data are generated from underlying parameters. It fits parameters to observed data to explain patterns or make predictions. Example: in Glicko, the statistical model assumes each player’s skill is a parameter and observed match outcomes inform updates to those skill estimates.

nodes.label: Confidence Interval
nodes.description: Derived from the Gaussian (normal) distribution: for a variable X∼N(μ,σ²), about 95% of values lie within ±1.96σ of the mean. A 95% confidence interval around an estimate μ is therefore (μ – 1.96·σ, μ + 1.96·σ). This means we are 95% confident that the true value (e.g., a player’s skill) lies within this range. Example: a Glicko rating r=1850 with RD=50 (σ=50) gives CI ≈ (1850 – 1.96·50, 1850 + 1.96·50) ≈ (1752, 1948), so we’re 95% confident the player’s true skill is between 1752 and 1948. Wider σ yields wider intervals, reflecting greater uncertainty.

nodes.label: Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM 2)
nodes.description:
SAM 2 is a unified foundation model for promptable segmentation in both images and videos.  It extends the original <node id="10">SAM</node> architecture by adding a lightweight streaming-memory module that retains object “memories” (spatial feature maps + semantic pointers) from previous frames, enabling real-time, interactive mask propagation and refinement across arbitrarily long videos.

• **Streaming Memory for Video** – introduces a FIFO memory bank of past frame embeddings and mask pointers, cross-attended at each frame to fuse temporal context without per-video fine-tuning.
• **Promptable Visual Segmentation (PVS) Task** – defines a general interactive segmentation task over video (“masklets”) using clicks, boxes or masks on any frame, unifying image and video segmentation under one interface.
• **Data Engine & SA-V Dataset** – builds a model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline to collect 35.5 M masks across 50.9 K videos (manual + auto), 53× larger than any prior VOS dataset, with minimal semantic constraints.
• **Transformer-Based Architecture** – adapts SAM’s mask decoder to videos via hierarchical image encoder (MAE-pretrained Hiera) + memory-attention blocks, supporting real-time inference (43.8 FPS on A100) at 1024² resolution.
• **Zero-Shot & Interactive Performance** – outperforms prior video segmentation systems (XMem++, Cutie) with >3× fewer interactions, and exceeds SAM on 37 zero-shot image benchmarks (1 click mIoU 61.9% vs 58.1%) while being 6× faster.

Originally published as “arXiv:2408.00714v2 [cs.CV] (Oct 2024)” by Nikhila Ravi et al., Meta FAIR.

nodes.label: Segment Anything (SAM)
nodes.description:
Segment Anything (SAM) is a promptable foundation model for image segmentation that, when given user prompts (points, boxes, masks or text), produces valid segmentation masks in real time without any downstream fine-tuning.

:
• **Promptable Segmentation Task** – formulates segmentation as a “promptable” task, where any spatial or textual cue can be used to specify what to segment, enabling zero-shot transfer via prompt engineering.
• **Efficient Model Architecture** – designs SAM as a heavy Vision Transformer image encoder + lightweight prompt encoder + mask decoder that runs in ∼50 ms per prompt and outputs multiple ambiguity-aware masks with confidence scores.
• **Data Engine & SA-1B Dataset** – introduces a model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline (assisted-manual → semi-automatic → fully-automatic) to collect over 1.1 billion masks on 11 million licensed, privacy-protected images.
• **Largest Segmentation Dataset** – releases SA-1B with 1.1 B high-quality masks, 11 M high-resolution images, privacy safeguards (blurred faces/license plates), and broad geographic diversity.
• **Extensive Zero-Shot Evaluation** – demonstrates SAM’s competitive or superior zero-shot performance on 23 segmentation benchmarks, edge detection, object proposals, instance segmentation, and text-to-mask tasks.

Originally published as “arXiv:2304.02643v1 [cs.CV] (Apr 2023)” by Alexander Kirillov et al., Meta AI Research.

nodes.label: Streaming Memory
nodes.description:
Streaming Memory keeps a fixed-size FIFO buffer of the last N frames’ image embeddings and mask tokens. Each incoming frame:
  1. Drops the oldest slot and appends its new features and mask pointers
  2. Cross-attends into this rolling window to fuse only recent context
  3. Writes back updated keys & mask tokens for future frames

This design lets SAM 2:
• **Use constant compute & RAM** per frame—no matter how long the video, each step costs the same
• **Smooth predictions** by leveraging only the most relevant recent history (cuts down flicker/jitter)
• **Propagate interactive prompts** through time so a click or box on one frame automatically refines masks in later frames without re-prompting

nodes.label: Transformer
nodes.description:
**What it is:** Transformers are a deep learning architecture built around self-attention, which lets every element in an input sequence (e.g., words, image patches, frame features) directly attend to every other element. Each layer has:

• **Multi-Head Self-Attention:** computes pairwise interactions between all tokens in parallel, capturing long-range dependencies efficiently.  
• **Position-Wise Feed-Forward Networks:** apply a small MLP to each token independently to mix features.  
• **Positional Encodings:** inject order or spatial information since attention itself is permutation-invariant.

**How it works:** Given a sequence of embeddings, self-attention produces new embeddings where each is a weighted sum of all inputs, with weights learned to focus on relevant context. Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel, allowing the model to capture different types of relationships. Stacking layers builds deep contextual representations.

**Why it’s good for SAM 2:**
• **Global Context:** attention spans the entire image or video frame, enabling precise mask boundaries even on high-resolution inputs.  
• **Parallel & Scalable:** computes all token relationships at once, making it practical for real-time inference on GPUs.  
• **Flexible Fusion:** cross-attention extensions easily integrate prompts and past frame memory, letting SAM 2 fuse spatial, temporal, and prompt signals seamlessly.

nodes.label: Deep Learning
nodes.description:
**What it is:** Deep learning is a subfield of machine learning where models—called neural networks—are composed of many stacked layers of interconnected “neurons.” Each layer learns to extract increasingly abstract features from raw data (pixels, audio waveforms, text tokens), enabling end-to-end learning of complex patterns.  

**Key components:**  
• **Layers & Neurons:** linear transforms + nonlinear activations wired in a directed graph.  
• **Backpropagation:** algorithm that computes gradients of a loss function w.r.t. every weight, driving learning via gradient descent.  
• **Representation Learning:** earlier layers learn basic features (edges, textures), deeper layers learn high-level concepts (objects, actions).  

**Why it’s good for SAM 2:**  
• **Scalable Feature Learning:** deep image and prompt encoders automatically discover rich embeddings from millions of masks and images.  
• **End-to-End Differentiability:** the entire prompt→mask pipeline (including streaming memory blocks) can be trained jointly for optimal performance.  
• **Flexibility:** supports complex architectures (Transformers, convolutional blocks, memory modules) that power SAM 2’s real-time, interactive segmentation capabilities.

nodes.label: Image Encoder
nodes.description:
Definition: A module that converts a raw image into numerical feature vectors summarizing its visual content.  
Why it matters: Downstream models (segmentation, detection, etc.) need compact, structured representations instead of raw pixels.  
Key ideas:  
• Produces spatially organized embeddings or feature maps that capture edges, textures, shapes, and context.  
• Balances local detail and broader context so later components can reason about both.  
• Is often pretrained to bootstrap general visual understanding.  
Relevance: Feeds downstream vision tasks such as mask decoding and object recognition.

nodes.label: Foundational Model
nodes.description:
Definition: A large-scale machine learning model (typically an overparameterized neural network) pretrained on broad, general data to learn representations that can be adapted to many downstream tasks. Its pretraining and interface often give it zero-shot generalization—performing new tasks at inference with no task-specific examples—and few-shot adaptability when given a small number of examples or prompts.  
Why it matters: It lets builders start from a powerful base and specialize behavior cheaply instead of training new models from scratch for every task.  
Key ideas:  
• Learns transferable features via broad self- or weakly-supervised pretraining over massive diverse data.  
• Is adapted to specific tasks through prompting, retrieval, adapters, few-shot examples, or lightweight fine-tuning.  
• Exhibits emergent zero-shot/few-shot capabilities as scale and data increase (zero-shot = no new examples; few-shot = a handful provided in context).  
Relevance: Serves as the substrate for systems like GPT, CLIP, and SAM, enabling immediate and efficient task specialization without rebuilding from zero.

nodes.label: Rolling Window
nodes.description:
Definition: A fixed-size sliding buffer that always contains the most recent N items (e.g., frame embeddings and mask tokens).  
Why it matters: It gives models access to recent history with constant compute and memory by keeping the lookback bounded.  
Key ideas:  
• On each new frame, the oldest entry is dropped and the new one appended, so the window ‘‘rolls’’ forward in time.  
• Fusion modules (like cross-attention) query only this bounded window to incorporate recent context.  
• Maintains temporal coherence without letting history grow unbounded.  
Relevance: Core mechanism inside Streaming Memory; provides the recent context that enables smooth, consistent video segmentation in SAM 2.

nodes.label: Buffer
nodes.description:
Definition: A temporary holding area for data in transit between a producer and a consumer.  
Why it matters: It decouples differing production/consumption rates, smoothing bursts and preventing stalls or data loss.  
Key ideas:  
• Producers write data into the buffer; consumers read from it.  
• Common forms include FIFO queues and ring (circular) buffers for fixed-size sliding history.  
• Policies handle overflow (drop/overwrite/backpressure) and underflow (waiting or fallback).  
Relevance: Core primitive behind the rolling window in Streaming Memory and used broadly in video, I/O, and networking to maintain stable data flow.

nodes.label: Machine Learning Model
nodes.description:
Definition: A parameterized function trained on data to make predictions or decisions by learning patterns; training adjusts its parameters to minimize a loss that measures error.  
Why it matters: It turns raw data into useful outputs (classification, regression, generation, etc.) by generalizing from examples instead of hard-coded rules.  
Key ideas:  
• Architecture: the chosen structure (linear model, tree, neural network) determines what patterns can be represented.  
• Training: uses data and an optimization algorithm (e.g., gradient descent) to fit parameters by minimizing a loss.  
• Generalization vs overfitting: a good model performs well on unseen data, not just its training examples.  
• Inference: applying the learned parameters to new inputs to produce predictions.  
Relevance: Builds on statistical modeling principles and is the basis for foundational models (like GPT or CLIP); used across tasks such as segmentation, ranking, and recommendation.

nodes.label: Feature Vector
nodes.description:
Definition: A fixed-length numeric vector that encodes meaningful attributes of an object (image, text, user state, etc.) so machines can compare, classify, or reason about it.  
Why it matters: It turns raw, high-dimensional data into structured inputs that downstream models can operate on efficiently and meaningfully.  
Key ideas:  
• Each dimension captures a latent feature or aspect; similarity in vector space implies semantic or functional similarity.  
• Often produced by encoders (e.g., image encoders, language models) and can be normalized for distance metrics.  
• Used for retrieval, nearest-neighbor search, clustering, classification, and as inputs to higher-level predictors.  
Relevance: Core representation used across recommendation, zero-shot/few-shot matching, and model inference pipelines.

nodes.label: Vector
nodes.description:
Definition: An ordered list of numbers representing magnitude and direction in a coordinate space.  
Why it matters: It is the basic building block in linear algebra for encoding positions, directions, and quantities, enabling combination, comparison, and transformation.  
Key ideas:  
• Components: each entry is a coordinate along a basis.  
• Operations: addition, scalar multiplication, dot product (similarity/projection), and norm (length).  
• Linear combinations & basis: any vector can be expressed as a weighted sum of basis vectors; changing basis re-expresses the same geometric object.  
Relevance: Foundation for feature vectors, embeddings, linear transformations, and similarity computations in machine learning.

nodes.label: SmolVLA
nodes.description:
Overview: SmolVLA is a compact, efficient vision-language-action (VLA) model that controls robots by fusing visual observations, natural language instructions, and sensorimotor state into continuous action chunks. It achieves high generalization and responsiveness on real and simulated robotics tasks while drastically reducing compute and data requirements.  

Novel Contributions:  
• **Lightweight multimodal backbone:** Builds on a pretrained vision-language model (SmolVLM-2) with layer skipping (keeping roughly the first half of layers) and aggressive visual token reduction to cut inference cost without losing critical perceptual signal.  
• **Flow-matching action expert with interleaved attention:** A conditional Flow Matching Transformer predicts overlapping chunks of low-level actions; it interleaves cross-attention (conditioning on environment features) and causal self-attention (ensuring temporal consistency) for smooth control.  
• **Asynchronous inference stack:** Decouples perception, action prediction, and execution via an action queue with thresholding and near-duplicate observation filtering to eliminate idle lags and maintain high control responsiveness under latency constraints.  
• **Community-driven efficient pretraining:** Trains end-to-end on a small, publicly contributed set of robotics datasets (∼22.9K episodes, 10.6M frames) to learn generalizable visuomotor skills, matching or exceeding much larger baselines.  

System-level Design: Uses sensorimotor state and language instructions to condition the vision-language model; projects and aggregates features into the action expert; predicts action chunks with overlap; and updates the robot via asynchronous execution.  

Relevance: Shows that open, affordable generalist robotic policies can be built by combining efficient foundational visual-language representations, flow-matched action generation, and latency-aware inference engineering.

nodes.label: Vision-Language Model
nodes.description:
Definition: A model that jointly processes visual inputs and language to produce multimodal representations or outputs.  
Why it matters: It can ground language in perception and enable tasks like instruction-conditioned control, image captioning, or vision-guided reasoning without separate pipelines.  
Key ideas:  
• Combines features from an image encoder and a language encoder into a shared space.  
• Enables zero-/few-shot task specification via natural-language prompts.  
• Often built on Transformer architectures to fuse modalities via cross- and self-attention.  
Relevance: Backbone for models that need to interpret instructions in context of visual observations, such as SmolVLA.

nodes.label: Flow Matching
nodes.description:
Definition: A training method that teaches a model how to fix noisy or corrupted data by learning the direction and amount of change needed to get back to the correct version.  
Why it matters: It makes generated outputs (like robot action sequences) smooth and coherent by letting the model gradually correct mistakes instead of predicting everything at once.  
Key ideas:  
• Create noisy versions of real data.  
• Train the model to predict how to adjust the noisy sample toward the original (the correction direction).  
• At inference, start from a noisy input and apply those predicted corrections step by step to produce a final output.  
Relevance: Used to train SmolVLA’s action expert so it can produce overlapping, stable chunks of robot actions conditioned on perception.

nodes.label: Asynchronous Inference
nodes.description:
Definition: A runtime strategy that overlaps perception, prediction, and execution so a robot never stalls waiting for new actions.  
Why it matters: It keeps control loops responsive despite latency by using already predicted actions while new ones are computed.  
Key ideas:  
• Maintains an action queue of overlapping action chunks.  
• Triggers new predictions early when the remaining queue falls below a threshold g.  
• Filters near-duplicate observations to avoid unnecessary recomputation.  
• Decouples execution from inference, enabling remote servers or staggered computation.  
Relevance: Core to SmolVLA’s real-time behavior; it prevents idle gaps and smooths control under latency constraints.
